claims.claim: Clute argues that the easy surface of Wolfe's prose can itself distract the reader from noticing that every word must be taken literally.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: may distract the reader from realizing that it can only
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute observes that the dwelling of a Wolfe narrator characteristically combines the functions of prison, pleasure garden and tomb.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: the home of the narrator of a typical Wolfe tale
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute adds that a Wolfe narrator's house is also likely to be a laboratory whose experimental subject is that narrator.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: the home of a Wolfe narrator will also serve as a laboratory
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute reads the first sentence of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as telling the reader at once that the text is a memoir that has been physically written down.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: we are meant to understand has actually been written down
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute states that academics have tended to avoid Wolfe for decades because his stories cannot be mined for detachable themes.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: academics have notoriously tended to shun him for decades

claims.claim: Wright argues that Severian is unreliable precisely because of the trait that makes him look reliable, his eidetic memory.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Mapping a Masterwork: A Critical Review of Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: unreliable because of the very characteristic that makes him appear wholly reliable

claims.claim: Wright explains the concealment in The Book of the New Sun as an effect of a narrator who remembers a wealth of detail and thereby scatters the meaning.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: remember a wealth of detail (plot) which scatters meaning

claims.claim: Wright names the gap between plot and story, the apparent and the real, as the signal that alerts the reader to Wolfe's game.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: gulf between plot and story, between the apparent and the real

claims.claim: Wright says the reader's first task is to see the text not as the religious document it claims to be but as the product of a manipulated narrator.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: the text not as the religious document it purports to be

claims.claim: Wright reports that on a first reading there is little in the prose surface of The Book of the New Sun to distinguish it from other genre novels.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: On a first, superficial reading, there is little to distinguish

claims.claim: Wright quotes Michael Bishop calling The Shadow of the Torturer immediately accessible to any reader of moderate intelligence.
claims.source: Michael Bishop, quoted by Peter Wright in 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: an immediately accessible book for anyone with moderate intelligence

claims.claim: Wright quotes Algis Budrys, a working novelist, saying he could tell the cards were up Wolfe's sleeve without being able to follow the moves.
claims.source: Algis Budrys, quoted by Peter Wright in 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: I know the cards are up the sleeves somewhere

claims.claim: Wright reports that Baird Searles's prediction of an academic field day over The Book of the New Sun had gone largely unfulfilled twenty years on.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: his prophecy has gone largely unfulfilled

claims.claim: Wright quotes Baird Searles calling the tetralogy a possible turning point of science fiction from matter to manner.
claims.source: Baird Searles, quoted by Peter Wright in 'Mapping a Masterwork', Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
claims.quote: from content to style, from matter to manner

claims.claim: Wolfe says he differentiates unlabelled speakers by giving each one something only that character would say, so the reader identifies the speaker from the content of the speech.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, 'Suns New, Long, and Short', Nova Express vol. 5 no. 1, Fall/Winter 1998; collected in Peter Wright (ed.), Shadows of the New Sun, Liverpool University Press, 2007
claims.quote: she is saying something that only Maytera Marble would say
